topic: Pain is not the same as damage

slides.headline: Hurt doesn't always mean harm
slides.sub: Why pain is a protective alarm, not a damage report.

slides.title: Pain is a protector
slides.body: Pain is your nervous system's way of protecting you. It's produced by the brain using many inputs, not just the state of your tissues. It's always real, but it isn't a direct measure of injury.

slides.title: Why the alarm gets sensitive
slides.body: When pain hangs around, the system can become more sensitive, like a smoke alarm that goes off when you make toast. Stress, poor sleep and worry can all turn the volume up.

slides.title: Scans don't tell the whole story
slides.body: Plenty of people without pain have disc bulges or joint changes on scans, and some people with a lot of pain have clear scans. The picture and the pain often don't match.

slides.title: Moving is usually safe
slides.body: For most persistent pain, some discomfort during exercise is OK and doesn't mean you're doing harm. Start small, build up gradually and check how you feel the next day.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: New pain after a significant injury, numbness or weakness, pain with fever or unexplained weight loss, or pain that's steadily getting worse is worth a proper assessment.

caption:
If it hurts, does that mean something's damaged? Not always.

Pain is your nervous system's protection alarm. It's always real, but it's shaped by many things, including sleep, stress and past experiences, not just what's happening in your tissues. When pain lingers, the alarm can get more sensitive, like a smoke detector that goes off for toast.

That's why scan findings and pain levels often don't match, and why gradual movement is usually safe even when it's a bit uncomfortable.

New pain after an injury, numbness, weakness or pain that keeps getting worse is worth an assessment.
